title: How to map a startup ecosystem with AI
description: Map startups, investors, activity, and relationships around a venture investment question with traceable evidence.
introduction: A useful startup map explains how a market is forming: which companies define it, where talent and capital are moving, who is investing, and which relationships matter. A long list of company names does not answer those questions.

Strawberry can inspect current company pages, funding announcements, investor portfolios, accelerator cohorts, databases in your logged-in browser, hiring, and news while keeping the evidence visible. Your firm's thesis, portfolio, and pass history can shape the map without being copied into a public research tool.

blocks.text: The scope changes depending on whether you are refining a thesis, learning a new geography, looking for white space, understanding capital flows, or preparing to source. Strawberry begins with that decision and the boundaries that matter: stage, geography, company type, time period, and exclusions.

items.context: Build a sourced startup landscape around the market question you need to answer.

sections.title: Map the system, not just the companies

items: Startups and the emerging categories they represent.
Investors, their evidenced stage and geography, and recent investment patterns.
Accelerators, universities, communities, and other sources of company formation.
Funding, founder, talent, partnership, and market relationships.
Changes in capital, technology, regulation, talent, or customer demand.

blocks.text: An investor's website describes an intended thesis. Dated portfolio and transaction evidence shows how that thesis appears in practice. Strawberry keeps the two separate, so one deal does not become a false pattern and a marketing statement does not become proof.

sections.title: Calibrate the taxonomy before going wide

blocks.text: Category boundaries are judgment calls. Strawberry starts with a varied cross-section when the scope is subjective, giving you a manageable view to correct before time and credits go into a broader sweep. You can refine which companies belong, which relationships matter, and how much evidence each row needs.

The finished map keeps source links and dates beside material facts and distinguishes classification from evidence. It can become a table, visual landscape, dataset, brief, or presentation depending on the decision.

Mapping and sourcing are related, but they are not the same job. A landscape explains the ecosystem. Sourcing applies the firm's thesis to create a reviewable set of opportunities. Research then deepens one selected company.

items.context: Turn the accepted landscape and thesis into a qualified first set of investment opportunities.
Build an evidence-backed view of one company that deserves attention.

blocks.text: Once the scope and source hierarchy are trusted, save them as a firm skill. A Routine can later refresh agreed sources and report material additions or changes without rebuilding the map from scratch.
